items.item: A lease is a promise from a quorum not to elect another leader until a deadline; while it holds, the holder can answer reads locally and still be linearizable, because no other leader can exist.

at.step: Reveal: a lease turns a quorum read into a local one

items.item: The lease argument's safety depends on the holder's clock and the granters' clocks drifting by less than a known bound, which is why the usable lease window is shortened by that bound.

at.step: Reveal: a lease turns a quorum read into a local one

items.item: A process paused longer than its lease, between checking it and acting, can resume and act as if it still held it; checking the lease again just before acting does not prevent this, because the pause can fall between that check and the write.

at.step: Reveal: why checking right before the write does not help

items.item: A fencing token is a number that increases every time a lock or lease is granted; sent with every write and checked by the resource being protected, it lets the resource reject any write carrying a token lower than one it has already seen.

at.step: Reveal: a fencing token, checked by the resource itself

items.item: Chubby's sequencer, Kafka's producer epoch, ZooKeeper's zxid, and Raft's term are four production names for the identical fencing-token idea.

at.step: Reveal: the same idea under four different names

items.item: A distributed lock alone is only a hint about who should be acting; mutual exclusion that depends on every participant's own timing is not safe, so safety must be enforced by the resource itself.

at.step: Reveal: a lock alone is a hint, not a guarantee

items.item: Chubby's lock-delay withholds a freed lock from other clients for a period after an apparent failure, as an imperfect defense for resources that cannot check a fencing token at all.

at.step: Reveal: a lock alone is a hint, not a guarantee

items.item: A unique but non-increasing token (such as a random string) lets a resource tell two writes apart but gives it no way to know which one came later, so it cannot reject a stale write the way a monotonic token can.

at.step: Prove it: a lock service hands out a unique random token every time — is that enough?

items.item: The storage layer rejecting a stale write is the only fix that survives an arbitrarily long pause, because it runs at write time, after any pause has already ended; re-checking a lease or lengthening it only relocates or delays the identical failure.

at.step: Predict: re-check the lease, lengthen it, or make storage reject the old holder?
